def: A short synthetic DNA sequence ligated to each fragment during library preparation so the sequencer can bind and read it. Adapter sequence that ends up inside a read is removed by trimming.

A p-value corrected for the number of tests that were run. In RNA-seq, thousands of genes are tested at once, so the raw p-value overstates the evidence. The usual correction is Benjamini-Hochberg, which controls the false discovery rate.
Finding where a read, or a whole sequence, best matches a reference sequence. Aligning RNA-seq reads to a genome needs a splice-aware aligner such as HISAT2 or STAR, because reads can span introns.
A file that says where the genes, transcripts and exons are on a genome, usually in GTF or GFF3 format. Counting reads per gene depends on it.
The compressed, binary form of a SAM file. It stores aligned reads and is what most downstream tools read. A sorted BAM file is usually accompanied by a .bai index.

Variation between samples that comes from how or when they were processed (different days, kits or sequencing runs) and not from the biology being studied. It can hide or mimic real differences if it is confounded with the conditions.
A tab-separated format for genomic intervals: chromosome, start and end. Start positions are 0-based, unlike most other formats.

An independent biological sample of the same condition, such as a different animal, plant or culture. Biological replicates measure real variability; a technical replicate only repeats the measurement of one sample.
Basic Local Alignment Search Tool. It finds regions of similarity between a query sequence and a database, and reports how likely each match is to have arisen by chance (the E-value).
Complementary DNA, made from RNA by reverse transcription. RNA-seq libraries are built from cDNA because sequencers read DNA.

A package and environment manager. It installs bioinformatics tools with their dependencies into separate environments, so different projects can use different versions without conflict. Bioconda is the channel that carries most bioinformatics software.
A continuous stretch of assembled sequence with no gaps, built by joining overlapping reads.
A table with one row per gene and one column per sample, holding the number of reads assigned to each gene. It is the input to differential expression analysis.
How many reads cover a given position, on average. 30× coverage means each base of the genome was sequenced about 30 times.

An R/Bioconductor package for differential expression analysis of count data. It models counts with a negative binomial distribution and shares information across genes to estimate variability from few replicates.
A statistically supported difference in a gene's expression between conditions, such as treated against control.
In a BLAST search, the number of matches at least this good that you would expect by chance in a database of that size. Smaller is better. It is not a p-value.
A part of a gene that remains in the mature RNA after splicing. Introns are the parts that are removed.
A text format for sequences. Each record is a header line starting with > followed by one or more lines of sequence.
The format for raw sequencing reads. Each read takes four lines: a name, the sequence, a separator, and one quality character per base.
The expected proportion of false positives among the results you call significant. An FDR of 5% means about 1 in 20 of your significant genes is expected to be a false positive.
The ratio of expression between two conditions. It is usually reported as log2 fold change, where 1 means doubled, −1 means halved and 0 means no change.

A structured vocabulary that describes what gene products do, in three branches: biological process, molecular function and cellular component. GO enrichment asks which terms are over-represented in a gene list.
Reconstructing a genome from sequencing reads, and also the name for the resulting reference sequence, such as GRCh38 for human.
Tab-separated formats for genome annotation. Each line describes one feature (gene, transcript, exon) with its coordinates and attributes.

Gene set enrichment analysis. It ranks all genes by how strongly they changed and asks whether the members of a gene set cluster at the top or bottom of the ranking, without needing a significance cut-off.
A data structure built from a reference so that software can search it quickly. Aligners need a genome index; samtools needs an index to jump to a region of a BAM file.
A short insertion or deletion of bases relative to the reference.
A sequence of length k. Many tools break reads into k-mers to compare, count or assemble them quickly.
The laboratory steps that turn RNA or DNA into a form the sequencer can read: fragmentation, conversion to cDNA for RNA, adapter ligation and amplification.
The percentage of reads that aligned to the reference. A low rate can mean contamination, a wrong or poor reference, or low-quality reads.
Adjusting counts so samples can be compared fairly, mainly for differences in sequencing depth and library composition. DESeq2 uses size factors; TPM and CPM are other schemes.
Reads sequenced from both ends of each fragment, giving two files per sample. They align more reliably than single-end reads and help with detecting splicing and structural variants.

Principal component analysis. It summarises the main patterns of variation across samples in a few axes. In RNA-seq it is used to check that replicates group together and to spot batch effects or outliers.
A per-base measure of sequencing accuracy: Q = −10 × log10(error probability). Q30 means a 1 in 1,000 chance that the base is wrong.
The probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as yours if there were truly no effect. It is not the probability that the result is wrong.
One sequence produced by the sequencer from one DNA fragment. An RNA-seq sample typically has tens of millions of reads.
The agreed representative sequence of a species' genome, against which reads are aligned and variants are described.
Sequencing the RNA in a sample to measure which genes are expressed and how strongly.
Sequence Alignment/Map: a text format with one line per aligned read, giving its position, mapping quality and how it matches the reference (the CIGAR string).
The total number of reads generated for a sample. More depth detects more lowly expressed genes, but replicates usually add more statistical power than extra depth.
Single nucleotide polymorphism: a position where a single base differs between individuals or from the reference.
The Sequence Read Archive, NCBI's repository of raw sequencing data. Runs have accessions that start with SRR, and studies link to GEO series (GSE).
Whether a library preserves which DNA strand a transcript came from. It must be set correctly when counting reads, or many reads are assigned to the wrong gene or to none.
Transcripts per million: an expression unit normalised for both gene length and sequencing depth. It is useful for comparing genes within a sample, but raw counts, not TPM, go into DESeq2.
All the RNA molecules present in a cell or tissue at a given time.
Removing adapter sequence and low-quality bases from reads before alignment.
Identifying positions where a sample's sequence differs from the reference, such as SNPs and indels.
Variant Call Format: a text format with one variant per line, listing position, reference and alternative alleles, quality and genotypes.
A scatter plot of statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value) against log2 fold change. Genes that changed strongly and significantly sit at the top left and top right.
